title: Reported speech
intro: Turkish has three everyday ways to pass on what someone said: quote it with *demek* (*“Geliyorum.” dedi*), attach a quote or a thought to another verb with *diye* (*“Neredesin?” diye sordu*), or report it second-hand with `-mIş` (*Geliyormuş*, he says he's coming). This unit covers all three, *diye* for purpose (*Bebek uyanmasın diye*, so that the baby doesn't wake up), and a first look at passing on requests: *Gelmeni söyledi* (She told you to come).

blocks.text: To quote someone, put their words first and *demek* after them: *“Geliyorum.” dedi* (“I'm coming,” she said). The quote stays exactly as it was said, person and tense included. In speech, *demek* often comes first, followed by *ki*: *Ali dedi ki: “Bu akşam sinemaya gidelim.”*

**Punctuation.** The quote goes in quotation marks, “ ”. In the style of the Turkish Language Association (TDK), the quoted sentence keeps its own full stop, question mark or exclamation mark inside the closing quotation mark, and *dedi* follows without a comma: *“Yarın geliyorum.” dedi.* *“Neredesin?” dedi.* Many books and newspapers put a comma instead of the full stop: *“Yarın geliyorum,” dedi.* Before a quote, a colon: *Öğretmen şöyle dedi: “Kitaplarınızı açın.”* Novels often set out dialogue with a dash at the start of each line: *— Nereye gidiyorsun?*

**Without quotation marks.** In speech, Turkish often passes on words just as they were said, and *dedi* closes them: *Ali yarın gelirim dedi* (Ali said he'd come tomorrow; literally, Ali said “I'll come tomorrow”). English changes **I** to **he** and moves the tense back; Turkish keeps the speaker's own words.

**Everyday phrases.** *Ne dedin?* (What did you say?), *Ne diyorsun?* (What are you saying? What do you think?), *Bu kelime ne demek?* (What does this word mean?), *Ne demek!* (Not at all! Don't mention it!), and *demek ki* (so, that means): *Işıklar açık, demek ki evdeler* (The lights are on, so they're home).

items.en: “I'm coming tomorrow,” she said.
My mother said, “Don't be late!”

items.tr: Ali dedi ki: “Bu akşam sinemaya gidelim.”
items.seg: Ali de|di ki: “Bu akşam sinemaya gidelim.”
items.en: Ali said, “Let's go to the cinema tonight.”
What did you say? I didn't hear.
What does this word mean?
Mehmet said he was ill, and didn't come.

blocks.text: *Söylemek* takes an object, not a quote: *Bana doğruyu söyledi* (She told me the truth). With *söylemek* and other verbs of speaking, a quote needs *diye*, as the next section shows; *demek* needs nothing else.

French also puts the quote first: « Je viens », a-t-il dit is *“Geliyorum.” dedi*. But where French reported speech changes the person and the tense (Il a dit qu'il venait), Turkish speech often keeps the speaker's words: *Ali geliyorum dedi*.

sections.title: “Neredesin?” diye sordu: diye after a quote

blocks.text: *Diye* is a form of *demek*, literally **saying**. It attaches a quote to any verb other than *demek*: *sormak, bağırmak, cevap vermek, yazmak, söylemek, düşünmek*. *“Neredesin?” diye sordu* is **“Where are you?” she asked**, literally **she asked, saying “Where are you?”**.

blocks.text: **Thoughts and fears.** The words before *diye* need not have been said aloud. They can be a thought, a worry or a check, usually without quotation marks: *Geç kalacağım diye korktum* (I was afraid I'd be late), *Kapı kilitli mi diye baktım* (I checked whether the door was locked).
**I heard.** *Diye duydum* passes on news you have heard: *Selin taşınıyor diye duydum* (I heard Selin is moving).
**Called.** *X diye bir …* is **a … called X**: *Kaş diye bir kasaba* (a town called Kaş), *Künefe diye bir tatlı* (a dessert called künefe).

items.en: “Where are you?” she asked.
“Help!” he shouted.
I was really afraid I'd be late.
I checked whether the door was locked.
I heard Selin is moving.
We went to a town called Kaş.

blocks.text: *Diye* already contains *demek*, so it never comes before *dedi*: *“Gel.” dedi*, or *“Gel.” diye bağırdı*, but not *“Gel.” diye dedi*.
*Diye* is written as one word, with an i, like *diyor* and *diyecek*.

After a verb in the third-person imperative ([A2 unit 7](gp-imperative-3rd)) or the optative ([A2 unit 7](gp-optative)), *diye* expresses a purpose: **so that, so as not to**. *Bebek uyanmasın diye sessiz konuştuk* is **We spoke quietly so that the baby wouldn't wake up**, literally **saying “let the baby not wake up”**. For **I** and **we**, use the optative: *Unutmayayım diye not aldım* (I made a note so I wouldn't forget), *Geç kalmayalım diye erken çıktık* (We left early so as not to be late).

blocks.label: Purpose with diye
lines: -sIn diye       so that he, she, it…   gelsin diye
-sInlAr diye    so that they…          gelsinler diye
-(y)AyIm diye   so that I…             unutmayayım diye
-(y)AlIm diye   so that we…            geç kalmayalım diye

blocks.text: For **you**, everyday Turkish prefers `-mAn için` ([B1 unit 4](gp-purpose)): *Üşümemen için sana bir ceket getirdim* (I brought you a jacket so you wouldn't be cold).

**Reason.** After an ordinary tense, *diye* gives a reason as someone saw it at the time: a fear, an expectation or an excuse. *Yağmur yağar diye şemsiyemi aldım* (I took my umbrella in case it rained), *Hasta diye işe gitmedi* (He didn't go to work because he was ill, or so he said), *Geç kaldım diye bana kızdı* (She got angry with me because I was late).

items.en: We spoke quietly so that the baby wouldn't wake up.
I made a note on my phone so I wouldn't forget.

items.tr: Herkes duysun diye yüksek sesle okudu.
items.seg: Herkes duy|sun di|y|e yüksek sesle okudu.
items.en: She read it aloud so that everyone could hear.
I took my umbrella in case it rained.
I came by metro because there's traffic.
He got angry with me because I was late.

blocks.text: For a purpose, the verb before *diye* is in the imperative or the optative: *Duysun diye bağırdım* (I shouted so that she would hear). With a tense, it becomes a reason: *Duyar diye fısıldadım* (I whispered in case she heard).

To pass on something you were told, without quoting it, add `-mIş` ([B1 unit 3](gp-mis-compounds)) to the verb: *Ali yarın gelecekmiş* (Ali's coming tomorrow, he says), *Ayşe hastaymış* (Ayşe is ill, apparently). The person changes as in English: Ali's **I** becomes **he**.

blocks.text: Every person works the same way: *Sen de geliyormuşsun* (I hear you're coming too), *Ben de davetliymişim* (Apparently I'm invited too).

**Naming the source.** To say who said it, put *diyor ki* or *dedi ki* in front: *Annem diyor ki akşama misafir gelecekmiş* (Mom says we've got guests coming this evening). On the phone and in messages, `-mIş` is the natural way to pass news on: *Murat aradı: toplantı ertelenmiş* (Murat called: the meeting's been postponed).

items.en: Ali's coming tomorrow, he says.
Ayşe is ill, apparently; she won't be able to come today.
Murat called: the meeting's been postponed.

items.tr: Annem diyor ki akşama misafir gelecekmiş.
items.seg: Annem diyor ki akşama misafir gel|ecek|miş.
items.en: Mom says we've got guests coming this evening.
I hear you're coming too. Is that right?

blocks.text: A quote names the speaker and keeps the words; `-mIş` keeps the news and leaves the speaker out. Both are everyday Turkish. The noun clause of *Geleceğini söyledi* (He said he would come) comes in [B2 unit 4](gp-dik-clauses).

To pass on a request or an order, turn the verb into `-mA` + possessive ([B1 unit 4](gp-ma-possessive)), add the accusative, and use *söylemek* (to tell) or *istemek* (to want): *“Erken gel.” dedi* → *Erken gelmemi söyledi* (She told me to come early). The possessive names the one who is to do it.

blocks.title: *gelmek*: she told me to come, you to come…

rows.en: she told him or her to come
she told you to come (plural or polite)

blocks.text: **Not to.** The negative adds a second *-mA*: *Geç kalmamamı söyledi* (She told me not to be late).

**To whom.** The person told can also be named in the dative: *Öğretmen bize kitaplarımızı açmamızı söyledi* (The teacher told us to open our books). A third person as the doer takes the genitive, as with *istemek*: *Babam Ali'nin de gelmesini istiyor* (My dad wants Ali to come too).

**Quote or report.** The same request can be quoted: *Müdür “Raporu yarına kadar bitirin.” dedi*, or reported: *Müdür raporu yarına kadar bitirmemizi söyledi* (The manager told us to finish the report by tomorrow). A wish about a third person is often quoted with the third-person imperative: *Annem “Ali de gelsin.” dedi* (My mother said Ali should come too). More ways to pass on requests, with *rica etmek*, come in [B2 unit 4](gp-reported-commands).

items.en: My mother told me to come early.
The doctor told me to rest.
The teacher told us to open our books.
I told you not to be late!
My dad wants Ali to come too.

blocks.text: The possessive shows who is to do it, not who was spoken to: *Gelmemi söyledi* is **she told me to come**; *Gelmesini söyledi* is **she said he should come**, or **she told him to come**.

summary: Quote with *demek* after the words: *“Geliyorum.” dedi*; or before them with *ki*: *Ali dedi ki: “…”*.
TDK style keeps the quote's own full stop, question or exclamation mark inside the quotation marks; many publishers use a comma: *“Geliyorum,” dedi*.
In speech, words are often passed on as they were said, without quotation marks: *Ali yarın gelirim dedi*.
*Diye* attaches a quote or a thought to other verbs: *“Neredesin?” diye sordu*, *Geç kalacağım diye korktum*; *Kaş diye bir kasaba* is **a town called Kaş**.
After `-sIn` or the optative, *diye* means **so that**: *Bebek uyanmasın diye*, *Unutmayayım diye*; after a tense, it gives a reason: *Yağmur yağar diye*.
`-mIş` passes on news without naming the speaker: *Ali yarın gelecekmiş*.
Requests are passed on with `-mA` + possessive + accusative + *söylemek*: *Gelmemi söyledi*, *Geç kalmamamı söyledi*.
